clue.text: dn's hazards for drivers?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as "dn's hazards for drivers? (4-5)": its opening is cut off by the OCR ("dn's" is a fragment), and no scan or search gives the missing words, so the wordplay cannot be shown.

clue.text: "Open" course?

parts.note: read two ways: a golf links in Kent that hosts the Open Championship, or a meal course served as bread with an uncovered filling

explanation.walkthrough: SANDWICH in Kent is home to Royal St George's, an Open Championship golf venue; an 'open sandwich' is also a dish served as one course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent town's links has staged golf's Open, and an open-faced version of this snack can be served as a course.

clue.text: More pleasant resort on river

parts.note: Nice is a resort city on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: A holiday town beside a river is the nicer place to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative synonym: something more agreeable or likeable.

clue.text: Lear's twentieth production in which Perdita appears

indicators.note: a production of a play suggests the letters being staged anew, worked into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A twentieth staging of King Lear, with a character from another Shakespeare play turning up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lear' tempts the solver toward King Lear, but LEARS and TWENTIETH are only letters: 'production' rearranges all fourteen into the play's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdita, the lost daughter of Leontes, is a character in this late Shakespeare romance, so the play is the one featuring her.

clue.text: Competitors go for gold in this sport

definitions.text: Competitors go for gold in this sport

parts.words: Competitors go for gold in this sport
parts.note: sounds like any contest for a gold medal, but the gold here is the yellow central ring of a target that bowmen aim at

explanation.walkthrough: The centre of a target in this sport is called the gold, so its competitors literally aim for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting arrows at a target scored in coloured rings, whose bullseye is gold, is the sport described.

clue.text: Humbug on tailless bear needs a detergent

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits on top of the next

parts.note: humbug is pretence or deception, a sham

indicators.note: a word without its tail has its final letter dropped

parts.note: Pooh is Winnie-the-Pooh, the famous bear

explanation.surface: A fake goes on a bear that has lost its tail and that needs washing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' drops the last H from POOH to give POO; 'on' places SHAM above it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Shampoo is a liquid cleaning agent for hair or carpets, a kind of detergent.

clue.text: Stone-work alongside a lake

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Masonry being done right beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone-work' reads as masonry, but the hyphen splits a definition, Stone, from the wordplay word work.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a gemstone with shifting iridescent colours.

clue.text: Say it, for example, at church

parts.note: 'it' is an example of a pronoun
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to speak a word aloud while in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' looks like the object of 'Say', but it is the word 'it', a pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: To pronounce is to utter or articulate, a synonym of say.

clue.text: Hurt, left before row arose

indicators.note: in a down clue a word that rises is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a row is a din, noise

explanation.surface: Someone was injured after leaving just before a quarrel broke out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arose' turns NOISE upward to ESION; 'row' rhymes with cow here, a racket, not a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesion is a wound or damaged area, so it is a hurt as a noun.

clue.text: County where choristers were trained

indicators.note: trained suggests the letters being drilled into a new order

explanation.surface: An English shire where a church choir received its musical schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Worcestershire is an English county in the West Midlands, home of the famous sauce.

clue.text: The Hole in the Wall" in scenic Hereford

indicators.note: the second 'in' says the letters sit inside the run of words scenic Hereford

explanation.surface: A pub called the Hole in the Wall in the pretty city of Hereford.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotes make it look like a pub name, but the definition is a literal recess in a wall. The opening 'The' and stray quote mark are link and print noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a shallow recess set into a wall, typically to hold an ornament.

clue.text: UCLA rooms turn out noisy and boisterous

indicators.note: to turn out is to be rearranged into something else, so the letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Dormitories at the University of California, Los Angeles, prove rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: UCLA is the University of California, Los Angeles; here it is only four letters for the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Clamorous describes a loud, insistent din, the racket of a noisy crowd.

clue.text: Solid piece of defence, say, against a general who is hostile

indicators.note: say signals that a word is spoken, so a sound-alike spelling is used

parts.note: a wall is a solid defensive barrier
Ike was the nickname of General Dwight D. Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A soldier positioned against an aggressive commander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives WARL, which in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like 'wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Warlike means aggressive and inclined to fight, a synonym of hostile.

clue.text: Highest wind possible?

parts.note: reads as the strongest gale, but wind means a wind instrument and highest means highest pitched

explanation.walkthrough: The small flute pitched an octave above the ordinary flute is the highest-sounding instrument in the orchestra's woodwind section.
explanation.definitionFit: The orchestral woodwind instrument with the topmost pitch is the little flute.

clue.text: German relative not at ease in the city

definitions.text: German relative not at ease in the city

parts.words: German relative not at ease in the city
parts.note: a cousin-german is a first cousin; the rest describes a rustic relation uncomfortable among urban sophistication

explanation.walkthrough: 'German' looks like a nationality, but 'cousin-german' is an old term for a first cousin, pointing to a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic relation who is awkward and out of place amid town ways is the phrase's meaning.

clue.text: Not having power to hold net up? That's insupportable

indicators.note: the outer word holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: lacking the power to do something is being unable

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper too weak to keep the net raised: the claim cannot be backed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns NET into TEN, which 'to hold' places within UNABLE, between UN and ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Untenable means unable to be defended or maintained, a synonym of insupportable.

clue.text: Light ale there is split

indicators.note: split means broken apart, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: Some beer has been spilled over there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means delicate and airy, extremely light in weight or feel.

clue.text: Competition keeping people up for 72 hours?

definitions.text: Competition keeping people up for 72 hours?

parts.words: Competition keeping people up for 72 hours?
parts.note: sounds like a sleepless marathon, but means a horse trial spread over three days with riders up in the saddle

explanation.walkthrough: 'up' is used of riders mounted on horses; this equestrian contest of dressage, cross-country and show-jumping runs over three days, 72 hours.
explanation.definitionFit: The equestrian contest combining dressage, cross-country and jumping held over three days is named for its duration.

clue.text: Denouements in which Watson finally signed off

indicators.note: says the next piece goes inside the shuffled word
off suggests the letters going awry, a disordered version of the word
finally picks the last letter of the word Watson

explanation.surface: Final chapters of a detective story in which Dr Watson signs off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges SIGNED to EDINGS; 'in which' puts N, the last letter of Watson, inside after the E.
explanation.definitionFit: A denouement is the final resolution of a story's plot, its conclusion.

clue.text: Trade, perhaps, with firm using architectural style of yesteryear

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the word may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: Business conducted together with a company working in an old-fashioned building design.
explanation.definitionFit: Art Deco is the geometric decorative design movement of the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Puzzle-maker observed after dance

indicators.note: the second piece follows the first

parts.note: a jig is a lively folk dance
saw is the past tense of see, observed

explanation.surface: Someone watched as a folk dance was performed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the tool: this fine saw cuts the interlocking pieces of a picture puzzle that shares its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrow-bladed power tool cuts curved shapes, and was used to cut out the interlocking pieces of picture puzzles.

clue.text: Fired with new form of dieting

indicators.note: a new form signals the word's letters recast into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone sacked for trying a novel kind of slimming plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignited means set alight, so fired in the sense of being lit.

clue.text: Willing to take tea, perhaps after the match?

indicators.note: after says the meal piece follows the match piece

parts.note: a Test is an international cricket match
ate means took a meal such as tea

explanation.surface: Ready to go for afternoon tea once the cricket is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willing' is not eager but making a will; tea is a meal taken in a break during cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Testate describes someone who has made a valid will before dying.

clue.text: District containing new stadium?

indicators.note: the outer word holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: an area is a district or region

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood that has a brand-new sports ground.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a large enclosed venue for sport or entertainment, like a stadium.

clue.text: Basic line-out producing sound of derision

indicators.note: out means put out of place, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A simple rugby line-out leads to jeers from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'line-out' looks like a rugby term, but 'out' is the anagram signal for BASIC and LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibilance is a hissing sound, as made by a crowd hissing in scorn.

clue.text: Girl caught in wire-netting

indicators.note: the letters are trapped inside the word wire-netting

explanation.surface: A young woman tangled up in a wire fence.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene is a female given name.

clue.text: Small dose of grass

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small
d is a pharmacist's abbreviation for dose

explanation.surface: A tiny amount of lawn grass is given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' is slang for marijuana, and so is weed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang names for cannabis.

clue.text: Jackson, no creator of a stir?

definitions.meaning: the Confederate general Thomas Jackson, known by this nickname
Lovelace's line says ... do not a prison make, and stir is slang for prison

explanation.surface: A general who never caused any excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' looks like a commotion but is slang for prison, recalling Richard Lovelace's 'Stone walls do not a prison make'.
explanation.definitionFit: General Thomas Jackson earned this nickname at Bull Run; per Lovelace's poem, the masonry barrier does not make a jail.
